theme: Pointing at the Other Side’s Strength
hindi: दुर्योधन द्रोणाचार्य से कहता है: “हे आचार्य! पाण्डवों की इस विशाल सेना को देखिए, जिसे आपके ही बुद्धिमान शिष्य, द्रुपद के पुत्र धृष्टद्युम्न ने युद्ध के लिए सजाया है।”
english: Duryodhana says to his teacher Drona, “Look, O teacher, at this mighty army of the sons of Pandu. It has been arranged for battle by your own clever student, the son of Drupada.”
deeper: Duryodhana is talking to Drona, the teacher of both the Pandavas and the Kauravas. He asks Drona to look at the enemy army. It sounds like a simple report, but he is also pointing out that the Pandava army is large and well organised.

Notice the words “your own student.” Dhrishtadyumna, the Pandava commander, had learned from Drona himself. Many teachers and commentators read a small sting in this. Duryodhana seems to be saying, “The one leading our enemies learned from you. Will you really fight him with full strength?” He calls Dhrishtadyumna dhīmān, “clever,” which can be praise, but here it also sounds like a worry he is trying to hide.

The lesson for us is gentle. When we are nervous, we may talk a lot, point at others, or try to push responsibility onto someone else. A calm heart simply looks at the situation honestly. This verse shows us a mind that is already uneasy, and that is where Arjuna’s own struggle later begins.
background: The Gita begins with the blind king Dhritarashtra asking his minister Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas did on the field of Kurukshetra (1.1). Sanjaya, who could see the whole battlefield from far away, begins to describe it.

In the previous verse, Sanjaya says that Duryodhana looked at the Pandava army standing in formation. He went straight to his teacher Drona and began to speak (1.2). This verse is the first thing Duryodhana says.
lessons: Duryodhana studies the other army, and honest observation is always a good first step.
Nervous people often talk a lot
Duryodhana’s words show worry hiding behind a confident report.
A good teacher shares knowledge with everyone who learns sincerely, even if they later stand on the other side.
Dhrishtadyumna arranged the Pandava army with skill, and good results begin with good planning.
Even a short sentence can carry praise, worry, or a hidden hint, so think about what you really mean.
examples: Aarav sees his classmate Nisha revising neatly with colour-coded notes. Instead of panicking, he looks honestly at how much he has prepared and makes a plan for the rest.
Before the match, Kabir tells his captain, “Look how tall their bowlers are!” He is really saying he feels nervous. The captain smiles and says, “Let’s practise our shots.”
Riya keeps saying, “The other team has the best singer.” Her friend notices she is actually afraid of singing on stage. Naming that fear helps more than talking about the other team.
Two students from different schools learned dance from the same teacher. At the contest, each wonders if the teacher will be fair. The teacher says, “I taught you both with the same love.”
Manav sees that another group has made a very neat chart. He admires the work and asks himself, “How can we make ours better?” instead of feeling jealous.
Sana’s team wins the kabaddi match because her captain planned each player’s position. She learns that a good plan matters as much as strength.
After a competition, Dev thanks his coach even though the winning player also trained with the same coach. He knows a teacher’s gift belongs to everyone.
When Tara forgets her homework, she says, “Everyone else’s bag is heavier than mine.” Her mother gently asks, “What is really bothering you?” Tara admits she is afraid of being scolded.

story.title: The Teacher Who Taught His Destined Rival
paras: Long ago, Drona and King Drupada studied together as friends in the same ashram. Later, Drupada became king of Panchala. When poor Drona came to him for help, remembering their old friendship, Drupada insulted him and did not honour his earlier promise.

Drona later became the teacher of the Kuru princes. As his fee, he asked them to bring Drupada to him, and they did. Drona took half of Drupada’s kingdom. Hurt and angry, Drupada performed a great fire ceremony and prayed for a son who could defeat Drona.

From that fire, the Mahabharata tells us, came Dhrishtadyumna, along with his sister Draupadi. Though Drona knew of Drupada’s wish, he still accepted Dhrishtadyumna as a student and taught him the art of warfare. A teacher’s duty was to teach, not to hold back knowledge out of anger.

Years later, Dhrishtadyumna became the commander of the Pandava army. When Duryodhana says “your own student” in this verse, he is reminding Drona of this old history. It shows how worried he is, and how differently Drona, a true teacher, could see things.
story.moral: Lesson: A true teacher shares knowledge fairly, and a worried mind should look at the truth instead of hiding behind clever words.

quiz.q: Who is speaking in this verse?
quiz.x: Duryodhana is speaking to his teacher Drona.

quiz.q: Who arranged the Pandava army in battle formation?
quiz.x: Drupada’s son Dhrishtadyumna, who was Drona’s student, arranged the army.

quiz.q: Why does Duryodhana call Dhrishtadyumna “your student”?
o: To point out that Drona himself taught the enemy commander
Because he wanted to make peace
quiz.x: It reminds Drona that his own student leads the other side, hinting at Duryodhana’s worry.

quiz.q: What can we learn from Duryodhana’s way of speaking?
o: Worry may hide behind many words
Never look at the other team
Fear is a sign of strength
quiz.x: His words sound confident, but they show an uneasy mind.

reel.hook: Why did Duryodhana tell Drona, “Look at the enemy army”?
reel.lesson: When we feel nervous, we may blame others, but calm honesty helps more.
reel.caption:
Ever pointed at someone else’s strength because you were nervous? 😟
Duryodhana did exactly that in Gita 1.3.
Today’s lesson: look honestly, prepare well, and speak from a calm heart. 🙏
